doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: Thinking process when improvising, and composition techniques
summary: Improvising becomes habitual; the same unconscious habits form in composition, and the principles are shared across all the arts.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: No, that’s okay. You know like when you take an improvisation out and you come back in.
Oh yeah, this is a C seven chord. All right.

The question of out and in, you played some things this morning, I should sort of describe, we were doing some things for the students under the auspices of our jazz professor Michael Woods. And I have this thing I do when someone plays something that I think is highly hip or unexpected or, in short, something I never would have thought of. And I find myself raising my eyebrows or, like turning my head. And you made me do that four or five times. And I just wanted to compliment you on the way you took things sort of out and brought them back in, and sometimes it happened really quickly. Is there a question here? There might be. Do you have a thought process when you improvise?

I think like any improviser it’s not on a conscious level. Things become habitual. You’re — manipulating parameters becomes habitual. You don’t think about the notes in a chord or a scale or which finger to push down to play when you improvise. But you think about the concept and the idea. But on the broader sense, not just playing an instrument and negotiating the changes, on a broader sense the same thing can happen in composition where you make it a habit of thinking consciously at first about texture, about displacement of rhythmic motifs by a different place in the meter, or augmentation. You know all these compositional techniques and you start to hone them just like you do a 2 — 5 — 7 lick and it becomes under your hand and you can spit it out in any key any

tempo, because you’ve got it. The same thing can happen compositionally when you start, you know you almost run through this checklist in a nanosecond about what’s at play right now in terms of composition, and then make decisions that are appropriate. That’s — I’d like to say that I aspire toward that. Sometimes it happens you know, but that I think is starting now. I think about myself as not an instrumentalist so much as just as a musician. And the same principles — that’s the cool thing — the same principles apply negotiating a jazz solo that apply to Palestrina or James Brown or Henry Moore or Becket. I mean it’s all the same — Debussy or Monet. I mean it’s all the same stuff and finding a commonality in all these things over you know centuries and centuries, thousands of years. And again, I took your question out a little bit and yes there was a question, but it’s not at a conscious level. I don’t think about doing things a little differently and affect it at a conscious level, it just sort of happens now. But to get to that point I have gone through the process of thinking about it consciously. I have a little advantage because I’ve been a composition professor for twenty years. You know, so I’ve gotten a release from having to run my changes, you know just play the changes over a solo. I mean I really have to think about this stuff slowly and deliberately with students, and consequently it goes into me more.
